title: Prompt slicing & morphology lab notes
content:
Context: quick personal scratchpad for experiments around prompt 'slicing' (breaking prompts into micro-templates), morphological variations (token-level surface changes), and how few-shot exemplar selection interacts with those changes. Goal is to produce a small library of robust templates and an error catalog for the prompt library.

Top-line takeaways so far (fast notes):
- Short, consistent anchors ("Task:") + explicit output schema drastically reduces structural failures.
- Morphological noise (typos, casing, punctuation variants) exposed brittle matching in our exemplar retrieval; performance drops unevenly across tasks.
- Few-shot exemplar ordering matters more when slice boundaries are ambiguous (i.e., long multi-part instructions).

Experiment matrix (high level):
- Variables: anchor form, slice granularity, exemplar count (k=0,1,3,5), exemplar selection strategy (random / nearest-prompt-embedding / stratified by error-type), morphological perturbation level (none / light / heavy).
- Datasets: internal instruction-following toy set (50 small tasks), customer-reported failure set (12 items), synthetic morphological-noise set (generated by edit ops).
- Metrics: exact-structure match (for constrained outputs), semantic-f1 (for free text), hallucination flag (binary), token-overhead delta.

Representative prompts used in tests (keep these short so they map to template slots):
1) Anchor-template (clean):
   "Task: Convert the following bullet points into a concise abstract. Input: <<BULLETS>> Output format: [one-paragraph summary]."

2) Sliced-template (micro):
   "A: Convert bullets -> summary. B: Tone: neutral. C: Max length: 80 tokens. INPUT: <<BULLETS>>. RESP: concise paragraph."

3) No-anchor (control):
   "Convert these into a short abstract: <<BULLETS>>"

Few-shot exemplar set (example used for k=3 experiments):
- Ex1 (format heavy): "Input: - X - Y. Output: [one-line summary]."
- Ex2 (semantic): "Input: - Foo A - Bar B. Output: concise paragraph describing the main point."
- Ex3 (contrasting length): "Input: - Long list... Output: one-sentence summary."

Observed failure cases (excerpts):
- Failure type A: structural miss
  Example: prompt included explicit "Output format: [one-paragraph summary]" but model returned a list. Occurred mostly in k=0 and no-anchor settings.

- Failure type B: hallucinated facts when exemplar style was too narrative
  Example: given bullets about product features, model invented a usage stat in the summary. Correlated with exemplars that contained numeric citations.

- Failure type C: exemplar-retrieval mismatch under morphological noise
  Example: when client text used all-caps headings, retrieval returned exemplars that were semantically nearby but stylistically different; results were verbose and duplicated lines.

Quantitative snapshot (toy numbers, for my memory):
- Anchor-template + k=3 (nearest exemplar): exact-structure 78%, hallucination 6%
- Sliced-template micro + k=3 (stratified): exact-structure 82%, hallucination 4%, token overhead +7%
- No-anchor + k=0: exact-structure 33%, hallucination 18%
- Morphological-heavy perturbation: structure delta -22 points on average (vs clean)

Hypotheses / interpretations:
- Anchors give the model stronger conditioning; slicing into labeled micro-templates improves structural compliance at a modest token cost.
- Few-shot exemplars should be selected not only for semantic similarity but for morphological/style similarity (caps, punctuation) to avoid style mismatch failures.
- When exemplar retrieval is noisy, increasing exemplar diversity (stratified by style) helps more than adding more exemplars of the same style.

Specific experiments to run next (prioritized):
1) Small ablation: anchor phrasing variants ("Task:" vs "Instruction:" vs "A:") across 100 tasks to quantify phrasing sensitivity.
2) Morphology-aware retrieval: augment prompt embeddings with a lightweight style fingerprint (character-level ngram) and test stratified selection.
3) Prefix caching probe: see if repeating an anchor in an earlier-in-sequence prompt reduces cold-start variance for burst requests.
4) Minimal formatted schema enforcement: try giving an explicit example output token (e.g., start token "<SUMMARY>") and see if exact-structure improves.

Edge-case notes / anecdotal bits:
- One customer case: their saved prompt used non-breaking spaces (UTF-160) — retrieval and tokenization differences caused a silent failure where the anchor wasn't matched. Add a normalizer for whitespace types.
- Avoid exemplars with metrics or dates unless we want the model to mimic that behavior; numbers seem to be a common hallucination trigger when examples include them.

Tooling ideas for prompt library:
- Store small "style fingerprints" with each exemplar (caps ratio, avg sentence length, punctuation density).
- Tag exemplars with explicit "do_not_copy_literals" when they contain customer-specific tokens (IDs, dates).
- Provide a quick 'probe' endpoint that runs 3 micro-variants of the prompt and returns a compact diff so engineers can choose stable template.

Open questions / TODOs (notes to self):
- How stable are these results across larger models (we've been using core-13B; need to check prod-70B and quantized variants).
- Is there a systematic way to generate morphological-noise that mirrors customer data? Current synthetic edits might not match real-world typos.
- Confirm whether exemplar retrieval latency increases significantly when adding style fingerprints.

Quick checklist before sharing with team:
- [ ] Run anchor phrasing ablation (30 tasks, 3 seeds)
- [ ] Add whitespace normalization to retrieval preproc
- [ ] Draft short internal doc summarizing the 'style fingerprint' idea for Console UX (for showing exemplar style)
- [ ] Attach example failure snippets to JIRA-ML-210

Links / pointers (for follow-up):
- PR with initial exemplar-style-indexing: https://github.com/redwood-inference/priming-experiments/pull/45
- Related confluence note: CONFLUENCE-PRIMING-42
- Jira ticket tracking noise experiments: JIRA-ML-210

Notes to self: keep this doc informal. Save iterations with dates when I run the next ablation.

Latest provisional labels: "prompt-slice-v1" (candidate template set) and "style-fingerprint-proto" (retrieval augment).
